    • Sources indicate that paretsky’s newest book, Bad Manufacturer, introduces a protagonist more in line with her age: Lily Sedaka, a former CIA field agent now in her seventies.
    • Paretsky will continue writing novels about Warshawski, but this fresh character will enable the author to tap into her own lived experiences—complete with the aches and pains that come with age.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that for more than four decades, V.I. Warshawski, the fictional private investigator created by Sara Paretsky, has aged slowly. In her late twenties and early thirties in the first novels, Warshawski is now about fifty years old. Unfortunately for Paretsky and the rest of us, time has flown by at a normal pace. In her mid-thirties when she published her first novel, Indemnity Only, in 1982, Paretsky is now seventy-nine and has less in common with her more youthful character.

    Sources indicate that paretsky’s newest book, Bad Manufacturer, introduces a protagonist more in line with her age: Lily Sedaka, a former CIA field agent now in her seventies. The book marks her twenty-fifth novel and the first non-Warshawski novel since Ghost Country in 1998.

    Paretsky will continue writing novels about Warshawski, but this fresh character will enable the author to tap into her own lived experiences—complete with the aches and pains that come with age.

    It has been revealed that like her Warshawski novels, Bad Organization takes place in Chicago but with an added worldview. Sections are set in the fictional Central Asian country of Hayalistan, where Sedaka once was stationed. In an interview conducted over Zoom, Paretsky reflected on the decision to introduce a latest character and the difficulty that came with inventing a language.

    L. Wayne Hicks: I wanted to ask you what made you decide to unveil a new character after so much success with the V.I. Warshawski novels.

    According to recent reports, sara Paretsky: Oh, you know, it wasn’t a deliberate decision. But she came to me. I was on vacation in Paris, which makes me sound more glamorous than I am. But especially because what happened was that I fell out of bed, which is totally not glamorous. And as I was rubbing my sore hip, I was thinking, what would happen if V.I. got to be my age, seventy-something, and injured herself and could no longer race around the streets after bad guys? And then I thought, I really don’t want V.I. to be old and creaky. I want her to stay kind of fifty-ish.

    It has been revealed that and really, in that moment, Lily came to me with her name, Lily, this ex-CIA agent who now was on the run from the CIA. The whole storyline took years to develop, and many false starts, but that was how it happened.

    LWH: Is Lily going to be a recurring character?

    Recent findings suggest that SP: I hope so. You know, everything depends on my being able to write faster than I do because I’m under contract to do a upcoming book in the V.I. series. I wrote 10,000 words that I threw out. I wrote ten thousand more words and threw out eight thousand. But I’ve started a file on Lily. I have a storyline that I’m really excited about for her that is totally hers. It’s not the kind of thing V.I. would be involved with.

    LWH: I was wondering since Lily and V.I are both in Chicago, whether there’d ever be a crossover or meetup.

    In a recent development, SP: That’s a delicate question. I don’t know if I should say this or not. I mean, I don’t know if this is politically advisable to say this, but Disney owns the rights in perpetuity to V.I. and any characters that hover around her. So, I want to own Lily, and that means that much as I would like to have a lot of crossover, that’s just not going to happen.

    LWH: Okay, and Disney has the rights because of the movie? (The 1991 film V.I. Warshawski, starring Kathleen Turner.).

    Industry observers note that SP: Yes, exactly. And I was young, ignorant, relied on advice. It wasn’t great advice, and here I am.

    LWH: Do you feel more of a kinship to Lily than you do to V.I. since you’re both in your seventies?

    SP: When V.I. and I were the same age, I don’t think I felt a kinship with her. I was thinking about that this morning. I have a cousin who’s my age, whom I admire greatly. I love her. She’s a wonderful woman in every way. She’s kind of more like V.I. She just got back from backpacking, carrying a thirty-pound backpack through the Boundary Waters in northern Minnesota, and she’s done many wonderful things in her life for women, so I admire her and I admire V.I. in that way.

    But I have to say that I actually actively envy Lily. I would like to be Lily. I never wanted to be V.I. I’d like to be that person who could insert herself into groups the way she did when she was actively working as a CIA agent. She scampers up and down mountains. She bathes naked with local women under the full moon and the glacier waters in the country where she worked.

    In a recent development, and I mean, like V.I., she takes a lot of risks, but unlike V.I., she’s a team player to a certain extent, insofar as the CIA lets her have a team, and then she’s got these incredible linguistic gifts, so I would like to be Lily, whereas I don’t want to be my cousin. I just like to admire my cousin.

    LWH: And you had to create an entirely fictional country for Lily to have had her adventures in.

    SP: Yes, I realized if I was going to write a book that was set in the CIA world, sort of set in the CIA world, if I wrote about any of the things that the CIA has really been involved with, I would spend the rest of my life answering letters from people who said, “Well, you got this detail on, and I was there from 1950 to 1990,” and so I thought, okay, the way around that is to create my own country, and then created my own language.

    That was a mistake because when the audio recorder was doing the reading, they mentioned there are sixty words in the Hayali language that are in the book that they needed to know how to pronounce. And I’m looking at them and thinking, why did I create a language that was Qs, Zs, and Ws? I don’t know how to pronounce these words. Figure it out yourself. But anyway, I made a stab at it, and I thought, well, if I ever do that again, it’s going to be a language that looks like French.

    LWH: You could have made Lily a retired CIA agent who doesn’t have a lot of health complications. She doesn’t have a bum shoulder. But you gave her things that people in their seventies would be going through. Is that just to make it more realistic?

    Recent findings suggest that SP: Well, yes, and you know it’s sort of a reflection of my own lived experience. I feel lucky to be in as good shape as I am with eighty kind of lurking around the corner, but I was badly injured in a car crash some years ago, and I have residual problems that keep me from scampering up and down mountains, and I just think if you get to be my age and you don’t have arthritis or joint problems or something that’s slowing you down, you have lived a lucky life.

    Industry observers note that so, I wanted that lived experience to be something that people could relate to as much as I relate to it, or in the same way that I relate to it. We all have these problems that we’re dealing with, and yet people carry on. And I think that was what I wanted to do with Lily to show that you can just keep on keeping on, even when it’s not so easy.

    In a recent development, LWH: When you started writing the V.I. series, you and she were roughly about the same age, but you’ve made her age a lot slower than the rest of us mortals.

    SP: Right. It’s just one of her superpowers. I had no imagination about what that series would be. I didn’t know it was going to be a series. I wanted to create a woman detective who was sort of turning the tables on the standard roles for women in crime fiction forty-plus years ago.

    Industry observers note that I thought I would write this book and then I would go back to whatever else I was doing in my life, which at that time was selling computers to insurance agents. I don’t know if I would have made different decisions if I’d imagined that there would be twenty-three more books about V.I. coming down the pike.

    It has been revealed that I’m not sure when you’re thirty that you can imagine seventy. I looked at my mother who had terrible health complications. She was in her fifties then, and I thought, oh well, you know, it’s just a question of taking care of yourself. And then I got to be fifty and had my own issues. Life gives you these slaps in the face to tell you to stop being so arrogant.

    LWH: Why do you think it was important to have Lily suffering from some of the physical ailments that she does versus making her full of vim and vigor and in great physical shape?

    In a recent development, SP: Well, I want a character who readers can connect to. I think everyone second-guesses themselves. Everyone makes choices that they may look back on with regret, as Lily does. She’s thinking back over her long life of service and realizing that there were things that she just didn’t see. They were going on in front of her and she didn’t see them.

    It has been revealed that I hope people can see their own experience in her, even if their experiences are, I don’t know, in a small town in the Midwest, as opposed to hiking up and down mountains in Central Asia. They’ll see that fundamentally she’s the same kind of person they are and if she can achieve her aspirations, other people can achieve their own aspirations.

    LWH: What can you do with a the character in her seventies that you couldn’t or wouldn’t be able to do with with V.I.?

    Sources indicate that SP: One reason that I took a break from V.I. was that she was getting to be too much like me. Too worried, too feeling overwhelmed by responsibility, too much questioning her judgment. V.I. is supposed to be a lot more—I don’t know if carefree is the right word, but bold. V.I. is supposed to be bolder.

    Recent findings suggest that lily is effective, but she’s not bold in that way. She’s someone who is more emotionally akin to me, I would say. And I was letting V.I. get too much into that space, and it was—I don’t want to say destroying her as a character, but it was making her character less what I wanted her to be. Bringing Lily on board and letting her have that part of my emotional landscape now makes it possible to have V.I revert more to what should be her character.

    LWH: Does Lily being as old as she is make her sort of invisible to people and let her go about her skullduggery or whatever she needs to get done?

    SP: Yes. There is no disguise like being an old woman in America. I’ll tell you one of the things that I loved about Grace and Frankie in the first episode with Lily Tomlin and Jane Fonda, is they’re in a liquor store and they cannot get the attention of the person behind the counter because he’s talking to some young person and he just doesn’t register two old women and so they shoplift. It’s like: why not?

    LWH: There are going to be readers who read that Sara Peretsky has a upcoming novel out, but they might be upset that it’s not another V.I. story. Do you think there’s going to be appeal, that people are going to enjoy reading both characters, both series?

    It has been revealed that SP: Well, I hope so. I mean, I’ve had very good feedback from the people who read the book so far. It was published September twenty-four in England. They usually publish the same month as my American publishers, but for some reason they were two months ahead or six weeks ahead. But they sold out their first printing the first week it was on sale, so that that’s encouraging that English readers were willing to take the chance on a fresh character.

    LWH: There are many novelists who have died but their characters keep going. Robert Parker, his Spenser novels are still being written by other people, but Sue Grafton said no, the alphabet ends with Y. What is your thinking? What is your preference?

    Recent findings suggest that SP: Oh, I’m with Sue on that. You know, this is my voice. This is my presence in the world. V.I. is too much part of my life, and I feel the same way about Lily. There are other people who write better than I do. There are other people who write faster, more creatively, but it wouldn’t be my voice.

    Years ago, the Japanese took over the Macallan whisky tech giant. I was talking to one of the master distillers in the Highlands, and he mentioned that that Suntory was bringing him over to be their lead tester on their chemically created version of Highland whisky, and he said, “They have the Scottish water, they have the Scottish peat, they have the Scottish barley, but they don’t have the Scottish air, and it is not Scotch.”.

    That’s how I feel about my character. You might have the storyline, you might have the name, but you don’t have my spirit, and so it is not V.I.

    It has been revealed that L. Wayne Hicks is a freelance writer who covered real-life crimes for newspapers in Florida and Colorado, and has written profiles of many mystery writers including Sara Paretsky, Michael Connelly, John Dunning, Donald J. Sobol, and Stephen White.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Kit is the email marketing platform experts choose to grow their audience, deepen their relationships, and build a business around the work they love. For coaches, YouTubers, authors, podcasters, and other creatives, there isn't a better marketing hub to rely on to grow audiences, automate email marketing, and sell digital products — all within one platform.More importantly, there isn't a team more committed to helping creators earn a living. We're on a mission to help creators earn $1 billion using our creator marketing platform. We have always been 100% independent and 100% remote.We are proud to have built a product that our customers love, and we look for people who have enthusiasm and belief in our mission, vision, and values to join our team. We're also embracing AI thoughtfully — both in how we build and how we hire to ensure our team is adaptable, innovative, and ready for what's next.

    According to recent reports, kit's most established creators run real companies, with teams, large lists, dedicated sending needs, and a buying process that our self-serve motion wasn't built to serve. Because this part of our business is growing, we're looking for a Senior Product Marketing Manager, Scaling Creators to own how Kit wins, lands, and expands these businesses through a sales-assisted motion that sits alongside our self-serve product.

    Sources indicate that you'll define who this buyer is, write the story that resonates and wins with them, and build the GTM strategy to drive inbound pipeline for our sales team. When these creators choose Kit and grow on it, they build more valuable businesses, and that's the outcome this role exists for.

    This is a full-time individual contributor role ideal for someone who has added an upmarket sales-led motion to a product-led company before and wants their work measured in win rate and deal size.

    It has been revealed that you'll report to Christina Lhi, Head of Marketing, and work alongside two other experienced Product Marketing Managers on Kit's product marketing team. Together, you'll keep the self-serve and sales-assisted stories feeling like one Kit.

    You'll spend a lot of your time with:.

    Our sales leadership, on who we sell to, the deal toolkit, enablement, and win/loss.

    Account Executives and Solutions Consultants, on demo narratives, discovery, and technical and migration proof.

    Product, on packaging, rolls out, and roadmap input.

    RevOps and analytics, on how accounts get routed to sales, attribution, and pricing decisions.

    Creator Success, on case studies, customer references, and expansion plays.

    Demand gen, content, and events, on campaigns and events for established creators.

    First Week: Dive into our onboarding curriculum in Notion and learn Kit's product, pricing, and current positioning. Attend Get-To-Know-You (GTKY) meetings with marketing, sales, Solutions Consultants, RevOps, and Creator Success. Get access to our CRM, call recordings, and product analytics, and start listening to recent sales calls. Understand how product marketing presently works at Kit.

    It has been revealed that first Month: Shadow 15+ sales calls and talk with 10 established creators, including recent wins, losses, and churned accounts. Audit the sales content reps use today and how product usage currently routes accounts to sales. Set baselines with RevOps for win rate, sales cycle, deal size, and expansion revenue. Share a written point of view with the entire growth team on who our established creator buyer is and the three biggest gaps in how we sell to them. And an action strategy on how we can win these creators.

    First Year: Sales runs on messaging and tools you built, pitch with confidence and we drive 2X inbound MQLs from when you started. You’ll own and lead our channel strategy, setting the vision, driving cross-functional alignment, and partnering with Marketing to bring it to life. You'll run a quarterly win/loss program and share what you learn openly, build a clear path for sales leads on our website, and make sure launches that matter to larger accounts ship with both a self-serve and a sales-assisted version. Your work has a direct impact on helping Kit reach $100,000,000 ARR while protecting the self-serve engine that got us here.

    Segmentation and buyer definition: turning firmographic and product usage data into a clear picture of who to sell to and when.

    Messaging and positioning for a sales-assisted buyer, including competitive differentiation and objection handling.

    Sales enablement that reps actually use: demo narratives, discovery guides, business cases, and battlecards.

    Writing and storytelling that turns product depth into a business case a non-technical buyer can act on.

    Working with CRM, product analytics, and pipeline data to measure funnel conversion, win rate, and deal size.

    Customer and market/competitor research, including win/loss interviews and call analysis.

    Systems thinking: connecting people, processes, data, and tools to identify opportunities and build repeatable solutions across the go-to-market motion.

    Strong AI fluency: knowing when to leverage AI and how to build AI-powered workflows or tools that scale product marketing work, with human judgment and quality checks built in.

    Pricing and packaging input for a upcoming tier or add-on (nice to have).

    7+ years in B2B SaaS product marketing, including at least 2 years supporting a sales team selling to mid-market and/or larger accounts.

    Added a sales-led motion on top of a product-led one at a high-growth company, and can show what changed before and after with clear metrics.

    Built a deal toolkit and enablement program from little or nothing, and tied it to a sales metric like win rate or deal size.

    Ran a win/loss or customer research program that changed how a team sold or built.

    Ran an expansion or account-based program for an existing customer base (nice to have).

    Worked in email, martech, or the creator economy.

    You lead without a formal title. You align sales, product, RevOps, and finance on goals, trade-offs, and what success looks like, then keep things moving.

    You advocate for creators in decisions, and you protect the self-serve experience instead of pushing every account toward sales.

    You act with urgency and stay focused on hitting OKRs and owning outcomes.

    It has been revealed that you work in public. You share findings, drafts, and the reasoning behind decisions so others can build on them.

    You connect data to decisions, and you help others get sharper about using it.

    You raise the bar on quality and iterate toward it, and you shape how your team uses AI, from call analysis to keeping battlecards current.

    Experience in only self-serve or only enterprise sales. This role lives in the space between them, and you'll need to understand both.

    Recent findings suggest that treating enablement as a deck handoff. The work includes coaching reps, measuring what gets used, and revising what doesn't land.

    Wanting a sales playbook already in place. Much of this motion doesn't exist yet, and you'll be building it as you learn.

    According to recent reports, preferring to be measured on output rather than outcomes. You'll share accountability with Sales for win rate, deal size, and expansion revenue.

    In a recent development, needing extensive approval before acting. You'll be trusted to make calls on speed versus quality and to explain your reasoning.

    Discomfort with direct, candid feedback, especially from sellers on what's working in live deals.

    It has been revealed that we're 100% remote with team members across the globe. We work mostly on East Coast time—so if you're based on the West Coast of the United States, Europe, or Asia, you might have a few early mornings or late evenings. We do our best to keep things reasonable, but a little time zone juggling comes with the territory.

    Kit has standardized salaries based on position, no matter where you live. For this role, we’re hiring at our level 4 ($166,000). Level is determined based on experience and our interview process.

    We cover up to $2,280 per month toward medical premiums, with dental and vision premiums fully covered. We offer Health Insurance plans through Aetna.

    $2,000 equipment allowance for your first two years, $1,000 budget every following two years. Company-provided laptops are issued to every Kit team member and are not included in the equipment budget.

    Individual learning + development budget ($3,500/year).

    Creator meetup budget ($50/month) to connect with creators over coffee, lunch, or other in-person meetups.

    Childcare benefit up to $3,000 annually through JOON.

    Twenty (20) days of paid time off during each year of employment.

    Paid paid vacation: An after-tax bonus of $1,000 for taking five consecutive days of vacation where you’re fully unplugged from work.

    Two weeks of paid sick time each year, including mental health + well being days.

    Twelve (12) weeks paid parental leave and flexible scheduling in your child’s first year.

    Up to six weeks of paid bereavement leave, medical leave, and disaster after six months of employment, two weeks of each paid leave in your first six months.

    Winter Break Closure: Kit closes for a week at the end of December, giving everyone a collective break to enjoy the holiday season. Essential support services remain available, with teams coordinating to ensure coverage during this period.

    Four-week, paid sabbatical after five years with the team.

    Fantastic in-person or virtual retreats with the team twice a year.

    We usually receive a large number of applications, and our goal is to follow up with you within two weeks. You’ll hear from us either way. Here’s what you can expect from the rest of our hiring process:.

    Hiring manager interview (45 min).

    Note, the release has been updated to include a quote from the National Security Division.

    An eight-count superseding indictment was unsealed today charging Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi, a dual Iranian-Iraqi national; Mohsen Mohajeri, an Iranian national; and Mohammad Ali al-Hassani, an Iraqi national, with terrorism-related offenses for their activities in support of Kata’ib Hizballah and Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), two U.S. designated foreign terrorist organizations (FTOs), including their involvement in nearly 20 attacks and attempted attacks throughout Europe and the United States, and a September 2026 terrorist plot at a British Royal Air Force Base in Fairford, United Kingdom, where American armed forces were stationed.

    “Anyone who prepares a terrorist plot on a military base housing American servicemembers will be prosecuted by the United States government,” said Attorney General Todd Blanche. “The defendants listed in the indictment allegedly supported two foreign terrorist organizations, and al-Saadi allegedly coordinated with his co-defendants in the days leading up to the attempted terrorist plot. This Department of Justice will continue dismantling terrorist networks and protecting the American people from terrorist organizations.”.

    “This eight-count indictment reveals the determination of Iran to commit terrorist attacks in Europe and the U.S., including one plot that was recently prevented at RAF Fairfield, a British Royal Air Force Base where American forces were stationed,” noted FBI Director Kash Patel. “According to the indictment, one of the subjects is behind bars awaiting trial yet he allegedly sent coded messages to assist in future acts of violence. To date, the subjects have been allegedly involved in nearly 20 attempted attacks throughout Europe and the United States in support of Kata’ib Hizballah and Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (“IRGC”), two U.S. designated foreign terrorist organizations. This FBI will use all our resources to detect and stop such terrorist attacks as we’ve done the last 21 months – with over 1,300 terrorists disrupted and nearly 7,000 Foreign Terrorist Organization related arrests, up 1,057%. All those who threaten our homeland will get the message – justice will find you.”.

    It has been revealed that “Today marks a major disruption of an alleged global terrorism conspiracy,” noted Acting Principal Deputy Assistant Attorney General for National Security M. Scott Proctor. “No matter where they are in the world, the National Security Division of the Department of Justice will pursue those who target American citizens and American interests. My thanks go out to the prosecutors and law enforcement partners for their work on this case.”.

    In a recent development, “As alleged, these defendants helped orchestrate a campaign of terror on behalf of terrorist organizations affiliated with Iran that targeted Jewish communities in Europe and the United States, and the British military base, RAF Fairford, housing American service members,” noted U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald for the Southern District of Latest York. “Even after one of their co-conspirators was arrested and placed in federal custody, the defendants allegedly continued coordinating terrorist activity through coded communications and a network of associates overseas. The threat presented by Iran and Iran-backed terrorist groups to America and our allies is not hypothetical — it is very real. Our Office will not stop working to address and disrupt this threat, and to prosecute those responsible.”.

    According to the allegations contained in the superseding indictment and other court filings: Al-Saadi, Mohsen Mohajeri, and al-Hassani allegedly conspired to commit terrorist attacks in Europe and the United States on behalf of an Iran-aligned terrorist network, which included the IRGC and Kata’ib Hizballah, both of which are FTOs. Most recently, in approximately September 2026, al-Hassani allegedly orchestrated a terrorist plot at a British Royal Air Force Base (RAF Fairford) in Fairford, United Kingdom (the “RAF Fairford Terrorist Plot”), which at the time of the attempted attack, housed U.S. military aircraft and personnel.

    Al-Hassani and Mohajeri, both of whom were in Iran at the time of the RAF Fairford Terrorist Plot, allegedly relied on a network of contacts in the United Kingdom. Al-Saadi, who was imprisoned and awaiting trial on pending terrorism charges in the Southern District of New York, attempted to coordinate with al-Hassani and Mohajeri from jail by passing coded messages through third parties.

    Al-Saadi, a longtime operative of the IRGC and Kata’ib Hizballah, was charged in May for working with and on behalf of the IRGC and Kata’ib Hizballah, as well as other FTOs, for his involvement in planning and promoting approximately 18 terrorist attacks in Europe; and for attempting to bomb a synagogue in Upcoming York. The picture below highlights al-Saadi in front of an array of machineguns in a conference room with a map of the United States on the wall next to a list of “legitimate targets” (redacted here) identifying former and current U.S. officials.

    As alleged, among the individuals with whom al-Saadi worked to facilitate and carry out the European Terrorist Attacks were Mohajeri and al-Hassani. Mohajeri is an Iranian national and operative of the IRGC who coordinated with al-Saadi and al-Hassani to carry out those terrorist attacks with the IRGC’s backing. Al-Hassani, who is originally from Iraq, used his contacts and criminal associates to carry out terrorist attacks in the United Kingdom.

    The European Terrorist Attacks were carried out in the name of a purportedly new terrorist group with the pseudonym Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiya (HAYI), which is a front for Kata’ib Hizballah and other FTOs. Of the 18 terrorist attacks in the spring of 2026 for which HAYI claimed responsibility in Europe, seven took place in the United Kingdom, the most of any European country. The attacks involved arsons, explosives, and in one instance, a near-fatal stabbing in London of two Jewish men, including a dual U.S.-British citizen.

    Al-Saadi, Mohajeri, and Al-Hassani were allegedly personally involved in planning many of the European Terrorist Attacks, and al-Saadi and Mohajeri helped create and publish online propaganda videos of these attacks. For example, on or about April 6, Mohajeri and al-Hassani planned attacks while together in a room in Iraq with a map of London displayed on a computer screen. In a video of that meeting, al-Hassani told Mohajeri, “we need to get focused on London.”  An image of the video is below, with Mohajeri on the right and al-Hassani on the left. HAYI then claimed responsibility for six terrorist attacks that occurred in and around London starting approximately one week later.

    Sources indicate that on or about April 17, al-Saadi, al-Hassani, and Mohajeri allegedly directed an individual to carry out one of the European Terrorist Attacks in real time. Specifically, al-Saadi, al-Hassani, and Mohajeri, along with others, were in a room watching a FaceTime video with the individual who was carrying out the attack, which was projected onto a large screen against the background of the HAYI logo. Al-Hassani directed the perpetrators’ actions, including by instructing the individual on the other end of the call to execute the attack and directing that individual to take a lighter and “light one in your hand,” “light it,” and “throw the fourth one.” Al-Saadi recorded the attack in real time, while Mohajeri recorded al-Hassani and al-Saadi in the room as they directed the attack. A still image from Mohajeri’s recording, showing al-Saadi (circled in red) and al-Hassani (circled in green), as they directed and filmed the attack, is below.

    The next day, on or about April 18, al-Hassani participated in another video call with an individual carrying out an attack on a synagogue in London, with the HAYI logo projected on the background of al-Hassani’s screen. During the video call, al-Hassani directed the individual to “light it up like a Christmas tree.” The person on the video then lit an improvised explosive device and threw it at a building. An image from the video is shown below.

    In March and April — overlapping with the time that al-Saadi was co-located in Iraq with Mohajeri and al-Hassani, planning the European Terrorist Attacks — al-Saadi allegedly attempted to coordinate and carry out terrorist attacks in the United States, including by targeting a synagogue in Manhattan.

    Recent findings suggest that on or about May 1, following the European Terrorist Attacks, al-Saadi was arrested abroad and subsequently transferred to the custody of the United States to face prosecution. Al-Saadi has been in federal custody since his arrival in the United States. For approximately four months following al-Saadi’s arrest, there were no additional attacks attributable to al-Saadi, Mohajeri, and al-Hassani.

    According to recent reports, in August, however, al-Hassani allegedly directed and paid associates in the United Kingdom to conduct preparatory steps and arrange logistics for the RAF Fairford Terrorist Plot. On Aug. 22, al-Hassani paid one individual (Individual-1) to perform pre-operational surveillance of RAF Fairford’s perimeter and al-Hassani subsequently received videos of the area surrounding the base. In later communications with al-Hassani, Individual-1 referred to him as “Ali.”.

    In a recent development, in September, al-Hassani also tasked and paid several individuals to help him prepare for the plot, including by procuring vans and barrels of fuel, researching the purchase of chemical accelerants, including large quantities of potassium chloride, and purchasing metallic objects that could be used as explosive shrapnel. At al-Hassani’s urging, those individuals commissioned custom decals that they affixed to the vans to create the appearance that they were used by a fuel delivery business and a swimming pool supply business.

    On Sept. 26, al-Hassani allegedly tasked individuals to drive three vans, some of which were later determined to contain barrels of fuel, to the RAF Fairford base. That day, al-Hassani was in frequent communication with the van drivers, helping to coordinate their movements and directing them where to drive. At least two of the three vans, while en route to the perimeter of RAF Fairford, encountered a security roadblock and were not allowed to proceed on their intended route. Al-Hassani communicated with the drivers and occupants of the vans both before and after encountering the security checkpoint. In the early morning hours of Sept. 27, law enforcement authorities in the United Kingdom recovered three white vans to which the fuel delivery business logos were affixed and arrested the occupants.

    Recent findings suggest that while in prison in New York awaiting trial, al-Saadi has had phone calls with his immediate family members located in Iraq. As alleged, al-Saadi used those calls to pass coded messages to Mohajeri and al-Hassani in the days leading up to the RAF Fairford Terrorist Plot.

    For example, in June and July, al-Saadi allegedly spoke with his mother and sister about Mohajeri. During those calls, they referred to Mohajeri by various aliases, including “Abbas, Abu Daniel” and “Sayyid Abbas.”  Al-Saadi also told his family members that he owed money to Mohajeri and directed them to pass along messages to Mohajeri about “work,” a term al-Saadi regularly used to describe terrorist activity, including on social media posts and in discussions with Mohajeri about partnering to conduct terrorist attacks. On one of those calls, al-Saadi also asked his sister, “What are they doing about all our old work?” and asked her whether it had been cancelled or just put on pause. Al-Saadi’s sister responded that “it isn’t cancelled.”.

    In a recent development, on or about Sept. 24, al-Saadi once again spoke with his immediate family by phone. On the call, al-Saadi allegedly inquired about how al-Hassani, whom al-Saadi referred to as “Ali,” was doing. Al-Saadi’s family informed al-Saadi that “Ali” had been transferred to the “International Section.”  Al-Saadi then allegedly instructed his family to “give him [al-Hassani] money so we can do it.”  As described above, three days later, al-Hassani orchestrated the RAF Fairford Terrorist Plot.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    NBA superstar LeBron James is suing the makers of sports betting app Bron, claiming that it is intentionally ripping off his nickname. (Photo from Shutterstock).

    NBA superstar LeBron James is suing the makers of sports betting app Bron, claiming that it is intentionally ripping off his nickname.

    It has been revealed that in a federal complaint filed Tuesday in the Southern District of Newly introduced York, James said he has been known as “Bron” since he was a young basketball standout in Ohio. He alleges that PlayVision and its co-founders, Anish Gupta and Marc Zoghby, seek “to trade on” his “valuable name and reputation” by naming their app Bron.

    There is no other connection between the word and the defendants or any other feature of their app, James alleges. He also argues in the complaint that when the defendants launched a marketing campaign for the Bron app earlier this month, they used a video advertisement that incorporated an artificial intelligence-generated version of him.

    Sources indicate that “The AI-generated version of Mr. James sits in an NBA-style locker room wearing a basketball jersey bearing Mr. James’s nickname, ‘Bron,’ above the number ‘23’—a number associated with Mr. James and the one he at the moment wears on the Philadelphia 76ers—with physical traits that mimic Mr. James, down to his identifiable tattoos,” according to the complaint.

    Sources indicate that “Speaking in Mr. James’s voice, the AI-generated Mr. James scrolls through wagers on other NBA players in defendants’ Bron app,” the complaint continues. “The ad then urges viewers to ‘scroll to bet.’”.

    The lawsuit seeks damages and an injunction preventing the defendants from using the “Bron” name; James’ name, image and likeness; and voice.

    Courthouse News Service has additional reporting.

    A representative for Bron did not respond to the publication’s request for comment.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • John Green wrote this: “I fell asleep the way you fall in love, slowly and then all at once.”.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    John Green wrote this: “I fell asleep the way you fall in love, slowly and then all at once.”.

    According to recent reports, I treasure this quotation because it applies to so many changes and revelations, and it happens to be a really good description of how I fell into writing crime fiction. After a career built mostly on upmarket fiction or women’s fiction or book club fiction or whatever term is meant to describe books mostly about relationships, mostly by women, I’ve switched genres. Forever? Not sure. For now? Absolutely. Does it feel momentous? Kind of, yes. How did it happen? Slowly and then all at once.

    I’ve wanted to write detective fiction for a very long time. Years. As a reader, I devour it. For well over a decade, when someone asked me to list my favorite living writers, Tana French was one of the first names out of my mouth. She still is. In my mind, she’s the gold standard, but there are many other crime writers on the list, writers of the kind of book you read and immediately say, “God, I wish I’d written that.”.

    Why? When I think about this question, I run into that thing where you try to explain why you love something that feels so natural and second nature to love that you’re at a loss. It must be due in part to the way I’m fascinated by puzzles: word, jigsaw, logic, riddles, any knotty problem that doesn’t have to do with numbers.

    I’m drawn to intricately put-together things that also seem seamless. Poetry is like that, which is maybe why I started out as a poet. There’s a mystery at the heart of every good poem, a thing to unlock, language that flings open a window to a fresh view of what it is to be a person in the world. The tangled and cryptic made beautifully or tragically or terrifyingly clear.

    Also, I love crime fiction for the way it can mop its characters into the darkest corners and then force them to find their way out. Characters in detective fiction confront humanity at its most broken, and sometimes that humanity is their own.

    I’m especially fascinated by the perspective of the detectives, people whose life’s work is predicated on people hurting other people, whether it’s out of fear, jealousy, personal gain, desperation, or what can only be called evil. Imagine making a pact with the world to stare down what most of us try to avoid, evil and destruction, and to try to hold to account the people who have the audacity to hurt, to murder their fellow human beings.

    Detectives pick a side in a way that most of us never have to and they do their best to keep their feet firmly planted on the ground of right and just, even when that ground shakes under them.

    So why didn’t I write a crime novel ages ago? There are two reasons.

    Firstly, I’ve never had a lot of choice about what I write. I’ve never been a writer with loads of book ideas or one that claims, with deliberation, “I want to write X next.” There’s usually a single idea that comes out of the kind of nowhere that’s really everywhere: newspapers, encounters on the street, an overheard conversation, a weirdly blue sky or the way the light hits someone’s face. So many tiny glimmers and slivers that eventually coalesce into an idea.

    It has been revealed that I write what I’m given to write. I hate how woo-woo that sounds, but oh well. That’s the way it is.

    And secondly, I didn’t have a character. Nearly everything I’ve ever written begins with a character, one that lives and develops inside my head, sometimes for years. For me, the story emerges from the characters, not the other way around. And for a long time, I didn’t have a detective character, even though I really, really wanted one.

    But to get to the “slowly” part from the John Green quotation, when I look at my books that weren’t mysteries, I see that they were. There’s a mystery at the center of each of them and, in some of them, there’s a character who is actively seeking to solve that mystery.

    Recent findings suggest that A boy looking for his biological father. A young woman trying to discover the history of the house she’s inherited. A woman seeking out, however reluctantly, the person who set a fire that threw her world into heartbreak. Two sisters trying to uncover lost years of their mother’s life before it’s too late.

    Detectives who aren’t detectives. Mysteries that aren’t murders. Clues to follow. Red herrings. Scraps and shards and dark corners and someone taking the measure of human cruelty or courage or grief or love and picking a side.

    It has been revealed that which brings us to the “all at once” part: Lina Cordova. My detective. Well, one of two. Aaron Cash would show up a little later (God, I love that guy). But Lina came first. She arrived suddenly and then lived inside my head until she became a full-fledged person to me. Where did she come from? Beats me. Why then and not before? No idea. But I was super happy to see her.

    Industry observers note that lina is half-Filipina, half-white, like me. She has a Filipino doctor father, like me. She is fiercely in love with her people, her dogs, her home. So am I. But she’s not me. She’s way taller, for one thing. And worlds braver. I learned her like you learn a language, slowly then all at once. Before I could write her story, I had to become Lina-fluent. So that’s what I did. It was awesome.

    She had the same best friend, Helly, from childhood, through elementary, middle, high school, through college and Lina’s law school years, and into adulthood. Then, someone murdered Helly and that person was never held to account and Lina’s heart and her whole being cracked.

    For a long time, she lost herself. So, as so many of us do, she took her shattered self and her family home, to the small city of Sheppley, Pennsylvania, where she found herself again, and she became a cop. One whose ace in the hole is her dead best friend, the voice inside her head that pushes her, sometimes relentlessly, toward the truth. Lina talks to Helly and Helly talks back and of course it’s not really Helly, but, for Lina, it is.

    Lina is a mother. She has a teenage daughter and a son on the autism spectrum. She has an ex-husband named Joe, who is still her safe harbor in every storm. She has a dead mother she adores and a father with whom she and her kids live and who is grumpy and bossy and as solid as a lighthouse on a rock. She is drawn to pretty clothes and excellent coffee. She comes home each day to an old stone house, warm yellow light, kids doing homework, two Yorkies, the smell of her dad’s cooking, and peace.

    In a recent development, I like an edgy, brooding, jaded, teetering-on-the edge-of-some-personal-chasm-or-other detective as much as the next person, but that’s not Lina. (It’s not Aaron, either, despite his past, the sort people are lucky to get out of alive).

    Sources indicate that lina has her frailties: at one point, she calls herself a “soft-boiled detective” and she’s right. No emotional armor, no cynicism. She can’t help but think of even the worst criminals as not monsters but human, a fact that can make her job extremely hard and that also functions as her superpower. She’s the kind of person who watches a pregnant fox cross a road in front of her and feels so protective of it she could weep. She’s funny and piercingly smart. She is haunted, hunted like a fox by hounds, by the cases she left unsolved.

    All at once, I had Lina. And then, I had Aaron. And then, from these two people, all at once, I had The Trusted. Because in that way the world of crime fiction is like the world of any other fiction, at least for me, a place where the story emerges from the characters, spins itself into being out of who they are: their personal histories, all their little quirks and preferences and weirdness, their friendships, all their passions, the books they read, the food they eat, everything that scares or sustains them.

    Sources indicate that thanks for showing up, Lina. You, too, Aaron. Thank you to all my earlier books and the characters who allowed them to happen. It turns out, at long last, slowly then all at once, I got to be a crime writer after all.

    Marisa de los Santos is the New York Times bestselling author of Love Walked In, Belong to Me, The Trusted, and Falling Together. She has also published a poetry collection called From the Bones Out.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The eastern facade of the University of Pennsylvania Carey Law School in 2006.
    • Recent findings suggest that the case of a suspended professor at the University of Pennsylvania Carey Law School who claims that she was fired because of her race after making comments about minority groups would be better considered as a free speech matter, a panel of the 3rd U.S.
    • The three-judge panel in Philadelphia suggested that professor Amy Wax’s claims of retaliation for speaking about racial problems was more of a First Amendment issue, rather than employment discrimination, as she had argued.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The eastern facade of the University of Pennsylvania Carey Law School in 2006. (Photo by Jeffrey M. Vinocur, CC-BY-SA-3.0, via Wikimedia Commons).

    Recent findings suggest that the case of a suspended professor at the University of Pennsylvania Carey Law School who claims that she was fired because of her race after making comments about minority groups would be better considered as a free speech matter, a panel of the 3rd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals at Philadelphia said Tuesday.

    The three-judge panel in Philadelphia suggested that professor Amy Wax’s claims of retaliation for speaking about racial problems was more of a First Amendment issue, rather than employment discrimination, as she had argued.

    In her brief, Wax, a white Jewish woman, stated that Title VI of the Civil Rights Act and Section 1981 of the Civil Rights Act prohibit discrimination “on the ground of race” and “on the basis of race,” respectively, differing them from Title VII.

    She argued that the the University of Pennsylvania had an alleged double standard, allowing faculty and students to participate in what she called antisemitic demonstrations against Israel without consequences but punishing her for her commentary on race.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Today the Department of Justice declared coordinated actions against the Democratic People’s Republic of North Korea (DPRK) government’s schemes to fund its regime through the massive theft of cryptocurrency.
    • Recent findings suggest that “North Korea’s government bankrolls its rogue regime and illicit weapons program through cryptocurrency theft,” mentioned Principal Deputy Assistant Attorney General for National Security M.
    • “The Criminal Division, specifically the Computer Crime and Intellectual Property Section (CCIPS), and our law enforcement partners played the critical role in immediately freezing billions of dollars’ worth of stolen Binance digital assets before they got beyond law enforcement reach,” noted Assistant Attorney General A.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Today the Department of Justice declared coordinated actions against the Democratic People’s Republic of North Korea (DPRK) government’s schemes to fund its regime through the massive theft of cryptocurrency. These actions include the seizure of cloud-based infrastructure used in the FaceStealer social engineering scheme that has resulted in the theft of more than $400 million worth of cryptocurrency and the court-authorized seizure and restraint of more than $1.2 billion worth of cryptocurrency recently stolen from Binance, a virtual currency exchange.

    Recent findings suggest that “North Korea’s government bankrolls its rogue regime and illicit weapons program through cryptocurrency theft,” mentioned Principal Deputy Assistant Attorney General for National Security M. Scott Proctor. “Today’s announcement demonstrates that America will fight back against that corrupt regime’s effort to profit through cybercrime. The National Security Division will use every tool at its disposal to seize and return North Korea’s ill-gotten gains.”.

    “The Criminal Division, specifically the Computer Crime and Intellectual Property Section (CCIPS), and our law enforcement partners played the critical role in immediately freezing billions of dollars’ worth of stolen Binance digital assets before they got beyond law enforcement reach,” noted Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva of the Justice Department’s Criminal Division. “As the Department’s liaison to the digital asset industry, the Criminal Division promptly and efficiently used its expertise to immediately halt about half of this historic breach.”.

    “Cryptocurrency unfortunately has become fertile ground for North Korea to defraud victims and fund its malign activities,” said First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli for the Central District of California. “Today’s seizure demonstrates that America will continue the fight against rogue states who financially gain from cybercrime.”.

    In a recent development, “By springing into action at a moment’s notice, we worked together to freeze this massive criminal fraud in its tracks,” said U.S. Attorney Jeanine Ferris Pirro for the District of Columbia. “The North Korean regime may think they are sophisticated cyber criminals, but we have consistently met them head on, as we did here seizing more than $1.2 billion of their stolen assets.”.

    “The North Korean regime relies on proceeds from large-scale cryptocurrency theft to fund its illicit weapons program, stealing billions of dollars in recent years,” mentioned FBI Cyber Branch Operations Director Brett Leatherman. “North Korean cyber actors have used the FaceStealer scheme to aggressively target individuals in the cryptocurrency and Web3 sectors through deceptive social engineering tactics, resulting in the theft of more than $400 million in the last 18 months. The FBI remains committed to identifying, disrupting, and imposing cost on North Korean actors targeting the virtual asset community.”.

    Industry observers note that “North Korea’s FaceStealer is a highly effective social engineering scheme capable of deceiving even the most experienced technical and security conscious computer user” said Assistant Director in Charge Patrick Grandy of the FBI’s Los Angeles Field Office. “It exploits our trust in ubiquitous video conference platforms and valued personal relationships. If you can’t imagine a scenario where you might fall prey to it, you are not thinking creatively enough. The FBI is sounding the alarm to elevate awareness of this growing scheme, now aimed not only at crypto theft, but also the exploitation of the of the open-source software supply chain.”.

    Seizure of FaceStealer Infrastructure – Central District of California.

    Today, the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Central District of California announced the disruption of cloud-based infrastructure used by North Korean hackers in a highly effective social engineering scheme that the FBI is calling “FaceStealer.” The scheme, which relies on surreptitiously recorded videos and artificial deepfakes, has resulted in the theft of more than $400 million in the last 18 months and the attempted compromise of individuals involved in the open-source software supply chain.

    North Korean hackers known publicly by the names Sapphire Sleet, UNC1069, Dangerous Password, CryptoCore, Advanced Persistent Threat 38 (APT38), BlueNoroff, and Stardust Chollima have lured targets with invitations to video meetings delivered from accounts stolen from prior victims. Once a target joins the meeting, the hackers record the target’s webcam video and play a prerecorded video of a previous victim or victims known to the target, thereby simulating the participation of trusted contacts in the meeting to gain the target’s trust. The North Korean hackers also use super intelligence (SI) to develop deepfake videos of well-known and influential individuals often in the cryptocurrency and web3 industries that make the FaceStealer scheme even more effective. Here again, they use the deepfake videos in the meetings with targets to gain the target’s trust.

    In a recent development, during the meeting, the hackers then introduce a fake technical error into the meeting, such as claiming that the target cannot be heard, and provide a link or prompt to fix the error. The “fix” surreptitiously installs malware on the target’s computer. With the target’s computer compromised, the hackers can steal cryptocurrency or exploit the target’s access to other computer infrastructure. In several reported cases, the hackers stole cryptocurrency and hijacked communication accounts several months to more than a year after the initial compromise. As part of the scheme the hackers also accessed the new victim’s contact lists, social media, and communications apps to target the victim’s personal and professional contacts.

    Industry observers note that the North Korean hackers target individuals working in the cryptocurrency and web3 industries. Additionally, they have increasingly targeted individuals involved in the development and maintenance of open-source software with the FaceStealer technique, attempting to gain access to their devices and the software repository accounts they control. This targeting appears calculated to enable software supply-chain attacks. Pursuant to a federal warrant, the FBI seized over 900 webcam videos of FaceStealer victims.

    The FBI today published a report providing greater detail on the mechanics of the FaceStealer scheme, including best practices to protect against this scheme and steps victims can take in the event of a compromise. Additionally, the FBI created a website, www.fbi.gov/facestealer, to serve as a centralized hub for resources and information on the scheme.

    It has been revealed that the effort to disrupt the FaceStealer campaign was led by Assistant U.S. Attorney Khaldoun Shobaki for the Central District of California and the FBI’s Los Angeles Field Office.

    The Department, FBI, and Law Enforcement Partners Interdict More Than a Billion Dollars Worth of Virtual Assets Stolen From Binance.

    In a recent development, separately from the FaceStealer campaign, on or about Oct. 29, members of the North Korean military, referred to by the FBI as “TraderTraitor” stole more than $6 billion worth of virtual assets from the Binance cryptocurrency exchange. Since the theft, the National Security Division’s National Security Cyber Section, the Criminal Division’s Computer Crime and Intellectual Property Section, the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Columbia, and law enforcement partners have worked closely with virtual asset service providers (VASPs) to interdict the stolen assets. Collective U.S. government and private sector efforts so far have resulted in the freeze of more than $2.7 billion, with the Department having already obtained court-authorization to seize or restrain in excess of $1.2 billion of that amount.

    Efforts to trace, freeze, seize, and forfeit the stolen virtual assets are ongoing, as TraderTraitor actors continue to launder such assets through various cryptocurrency bridges, mixers, and exchanges. For example, last week, the FBI, in coordination with its law enforcement partners at the U.S. Secret Service (USSS) and the Internal Revenue Service (IRS-CI), issued a Cyber Alert attributing the theft and urging VASPs to block transactions with or derived from cryptocurrency addresses TraderTraitor actors are using to launder the stolen Binance assets.

    The FBI’s Los Angeles Field Office, Cyber Division, and Virtual Asset Unit are coordinating the FBI’s efforts to recover the stolen virtual assets, working in partnership with the USSS and the IRS-CI.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that kit is the email marketing platform experts choose to grow their audience, deepen their relationships, and build a business around the work they love. For coaches, YouTubers, authors, podcasters, and other creatives, there isn't a better marketing hub to rely on to grow audiences, automate email marketing, and sell digital products — all within one platform.More importantly, there isn't a team more committed to helping creators earn a living. We're on a mission to help creators earn $1 billion using our creator marketing platform. We have always been 100% independent and 100% remote.We are proud to have built a product that our customers love, and we look for people who have enthusiasm and belief in our mission, vision, and values to join our team. We're also embracing AI thoughtfully — both in how we build and how we hire to ensure our team is adaptable, innovative, and ready for what's next.

    Kit's most established creators run real companies, with teams, large lists, dedicated sending needs, and a buying process that our self-serve motion wasn't built to serve. Because this part of our business is growing, we're looking for a Senior Product Marketing Manager, Scaling Creators to own how Kit wins, lands, and expands these businesses through a sales-assisted motion that sits alongside our self-serve product.

    You'll define who this buyer is, write the story that resonates and wins with them, and build the GTM strategy to drive inbound pipeline for our sales team. When these creators choose Kit and grow on it, they build more valuable businesses, and that's the outcome this role exists for.

    This is a full-time individual contributor role ideal for someone who has added an upmarket sales-led motion to a product-led company before and wants their work measured in win rate and deal size.

    You'll report to Christina Lhi, Head of Marketing, and work alongside two other experienced Product Marketing Managers on Kit's product marketing team. Together, you'll keep the self-serve and sales-assisted stories feeling like one Kit.

    You'll spend a lot of your time with:.

    Our sales leadership, on who we sell to, the deal toolkit, enablement, and win/loss.

    Account Executives and Solutions Consultants, on demo narratives, discovery, and technical and migration proof.

    Product, on packaging, debuts, and roadmap input.

    RevOps and analytics, on how accounts get routed to sales, attribution, and pricing decisions.

    Creator Success, on case studies, customer references, and expansion plays.

    Demand gen, content, and events, on campaigns and events for established creators.

    First Week: Dive into our onboarding curriculum in Notion and learn Kit's product, pricing, and current positioning. Attend Get-To-Know-You (GTKY) meetings with marketing, sales, Solutions Consultants, RevOps, and Creator Success. Get access to our CRM, call recordings, and product analytics, and start listening to recent sales calls. Understand how product marketing presently works at Kit.

    It has been revealed that first Month: Shadow 15+ sales calls and talk with 10 established creators, including recent wins, losses, and churned accounts. Audit the sales content reps use today and how product usage at the moment routes accounts to sales. Set baselines with RevOps for win rate, sales cycle, deal size, and expansion revenue. Share a written point of view with the entire growth team on who our established creator buyer is and the three biggest gaps in how we sell to them. And an action proposal on how we can win these creators.

    First Year: Sales runs on messaging and tools you built, pitch with confidence and we drive 2X inbound MQLs from when you started. You’ll own and lead our channel strategy, setting the vision, driving cross-functional alignment, and partnering with Marketing to bring it to life. You'll run a quarterly win/loss program and share what you learn openly, build a clear path for sales leads on our website, and make sure debuts that matter to larger accounts ship with both a self-serve and a sales-assisted version. Your work has a direct impact on helping Kit reach $100,000,000 ARR while protecting the self-serve engine that got us here.

    Segmentation and buyer definition: turning firmographic and product usage data into a clear picture of who to sell to and when.

    Messaging and positioning for a sales-assisted buyer, including competitive differentiation and objection handling.

    Sales enablement that reps actually use: demo narratives, discovery guides, business cases, and battlecards.

    Writing and storytelling that turns product depth into a business case a non-technical buyer can act on.

    Working with CRM, product analytics, and pipeline data to measure funnel conversion, win rate, and deal size.

    Customer and market/competitor research, including win/loss interviews and call analysis.

    Systems thinking: connecting people, processes, data, and tools to identify opportunities and build repeatable solutions across the go-to-market motion.

    Strong AI fluency: knowing when to leverage AI and how to build AI-powered workflows or tools that scale product marketing work, with human judgment and quality checks built in.

    Pricing and packaging input for a upcoming tier or add-on (nice to have).

    7+ years in B2B SaaS product marketing, including at least 2 years supporting a sales team selling to mid-market and/or larger accounts.

    Added a sales-led motion on top of a product-led one at a high-growth manufacturer, and can show what changed before and after with clear metrics.

    Built a deal toolkit and enablement program from little or nothing, and tied it to a sales metric like win rate or deal size.

    Ran a win/loss or customer research program that changed how a team sold or built.

    Ran an expansion or account-based program for an existing customer base (nice to have).

    Worked in email, martech, or the creator economy.

    You lead without a formal title. You align sales, product, RevOps, and finance on goals, trade-offs, and what success looks like, then keep things moving.

    You advocate for creators in decisions, and you protect the self-serve experience instead of pushing every account toward sales.

    You act with urgency and stay focused on hitting OKRs and owning outcomes.

    According to recent reports, you work in public. You share findings, drafts, and the reasoning behind decisions so others can build on them.

    You connect data to decisions, and you help others get sharper about using it.

    You raise the bar on quality and iterate toward it, and you shape how your team uses AI, from call analysis to keeping battlecards current.

    It has been revealed that experience in only self-serve or only enterprise sales. This role lives in the space between them, and you'll need to understand both.

    A German beauty group that makes and distributes former soccer player David Beckham’s fragrance line has kicked out at the soccer icon’s lawsuit against them, asking a Latest York court to dismiss the case.

    The Associated Press reported Tuesday that German-based Coty has argued that the Upcoming York Supreme Court lacks jurisdiction, and that Beckham’s commercial entity DB Ventures is simply using the claim to “manufacture its early exit” from their deal to sign with another organization.

    DB Ventures had originally filed suit in April, alleging that Beckham’s brand of luxury colognes and fragrances were being sold at gas stations and discount stores in violation of their agreement.

    According to the AP, Beckham’s name is a famous global brand synonymous with luxury and elegance.

    It has been revealed that “Imagine, then, the shock and dismay experienced when DB Ventures discovered that David Beckham products were being offered for sale in a gas station,” the complaint said. “How could this possibly have happened? Desperation and greed.”.

    According to the AP, DB Ventures is seeking at least $41 million in damages for breach of its licensing agreement.

    According to recent reports, coty told the AP that it strongly disputes the claims and would not comment further on ongoing litigation. Authentic Brands, DB Ventures’ parent tech giant, declined to comment to the AP.

    Beckham, a former Manchester United, Real Madrid, AC Milan, Paris Saint-Germain and LA Galaxy player who captained the English national football team and was knighted in 2025, has built a business career that includes co-owning soccer team Inter Miami.

    According to the Sunday Times, he is the first billionaire sports figure in the United Kingdom, having a combined net worth of about $1.58 billion with his wife, Victoria Beckham, a former member of the Spice Girls music group.

    • A judge in Michigan was found guilty Monday of drunk driving after he rear-ended a public transit bus, but a district court judge ruled that prosecutors failed to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that his blood alcohol level met the threshold for the state’s original charge of a more serious offense.
    • Warren 37th District Court Chief Judge John M.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    November 18, 2026, 12:42 pm CST.

    A judge in Michigan was found guilty Monday of drunk driving after he rear-ended a public transit bus, but a district court judge ruled that prosecutors failed to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that his blood alcohol level met the state’s threshold for intoxication. (Image from Shutterstock).

    A judge in Michigan was found guilty Monday of drunk driving after he rear-ended a public transit bus, but a district court judge ruled that prosecutors failed to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that his blood alcohol level met the threshold for the state’s original charge of a more serious offense.

    Warren 37th District Court Chief Judge John M. Chmura, 63, was found guilty of intoxication while driving his Ford Fusion into a parked bus that was displaying hazard lights March 25. But the court rejected the charge of Chmura driving with an elevated high blood alcohol content of 0.17 or greater, according to coverage on Law360.

    Novi 52nd District Court Judge David Law noted that Chmura’s judgment had been affected, but he questioned the blood alcohol concentration at the time of the crash.

    Industry observers note that “This court may think it knows the answer to whether or not this was a high BAC case,” Law remarked. “But thinking it knows is not enough. It needs to be proven beyond a reasonable doubt.”.

    A bus driver sitting inside the bus waiting to resume his route was uninjured in the crash. Sterling Heights, Michigan, police officer Jonathan Journeau testified that Chmura smelled of alcohol, slurred his speech and couldn’t maintain his balance.

    Chmura’s attorney, David J. Kramer of the David J. Kramer Law Firm, argued that prosecutors could not establish the higher offense because Journeau failed to determine when the judge’s final alcoholic beverage was consumed.

    #147088. Supreme Court agrees to hear case on Trump administration’s suspension of asylum

    📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1561 w)
